---
title: "Overview of the models"
aliases:
  - /package/model-choice.html
---

METIS ships several model families. This page gives a high-level comparison
so you can pick a starting point; each model has its own page with detail.
All worked examples use the same [SIRDS model](../basics/sirds-example.qmd).

| Model | Stochastic | Training cost | Inference cost | Sequence conditioning | Exact density |
|-------|:-----------:|:-------------:|:--------------:|:---------------------:|:----------------:|
| [MLP](mlp.qmd) | No | Low | Low | No | No |
| [Transformer](transformer.qmd) | No | High | Medium | Yes | No |
| [Flow Matching](flow-matching.qmd) | Yes | High | High | Yes | No |
| [Normalising Flow](normalising-flow.qmd) | Yes | Medium | Medium | No | Yes |

Start with an **MLP** when you need a fast, deterministic prediction from static
inputs. Try a **transformer** when temporal structure or an observed sequence
matters. Use **flow matching** or **normalising flow** when you need to reproduce
variation between simulator runs; choose a normalising flow if you also need to
evaluate the fitted surrogate's density.

These compute costs are rough guides, not benchmark results. Compare models on
the same validation split, then assess the chosen model on held-out simulations
as in the [training tutorial](../basics/training.qmd). A more complex model is
only useful if it improves the predictions you need.

Sequence conditioning uses past observations in the transformer and the full
supplied path in flow matching. Exact density refers to the fitted continuous
flow, not the exact likelihood of the simulator.
